0. Overview of the lecture¶

  • In this lecture, we study more volatility models.

  • We start with GARCH models that generalize ARCH models (the same way that ARMA generalizes AR)

  • We then consider mixed ARIMA + GARCH model, where the mean equation is ARIMA with error that is described by GARCH
  • After this, we study several extensions of GARCH models that are developed to explain behaviors of financial return time series that the standard GARCH model cannot explain:
    • IGARCH: persistence of volatility shocks
    • GARCH-M: risk premium
    • EGARCH, TGARCH, APARCH: the leverage effect (Lecture 13)

1. Generalized ARCH (GARCH) models¶

  • ARCH processes can be very restrictive. You may need a high order ARCH process to properly fit a time series.
  • The situation is similar to what we faced with AR(p) models. To find more parsimonious models, we extended AR to ARMA.
  • In the same way, GARCH models extend ARCH.
  • If $\{a_t\}$ is a GARCH(p,q) model, then $\{a_t^2\}$ is an ARMA(p,q) process
  • $\{a_t\}$ is a GARCH(p,q) process if, for $t=1,2,\dots$,
\begin{align*} \begin{cases} a_t = \sig_t\,\eps_t,\quad \eps_t\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} F_\eps,\\ \sig_t^2 = \om + \al_1\,a_{t-1}^2 + \dots + \al_p\,a_{t-p}^2 + \beta_1\,\sig_{t-1}^2 + \dots + \beta_q\,\sig_{t-q}^2. \end{cases} \end{align*}

  • At $t=0$, we assume that $a_{0}, a_{-1}, \dots, a_{-p}$ are known and $\sig_{-1}^2, \sig_{-2}^2, \dots, \sig_{-q}^2$ are unknown random variables.

  • As in the ARCH specification, $F_\eps$ is any distribution function such that $\Eb(\eps_t)=0$ and $\Var(\eps_t)=1$

  • We assume $\om>0$, and $\al_i,\beta_j\ge0$
  • Under additional conditions, $\{a_t\}$ are weak white noise. However, $\{a_t\}$ is serially dependent and shows variance clustering
  • To obtain ARMA form of $\{a_t^2\}$, we define $\eta_t = a_t^2-\sig_t^2$
  • It can be shown that $\{\eta_t\}$ is a weak white noise
  • By some calculations, one can show that
\begin{align*} a_t^2 = \om + \sum_{i=1}^{\max(p,q)} (\al_i+\beta_i) a_{t-i}^2 + \eta_t -\sum_{j=1}^q \beta_j \eta_{t-j} \end{align*}
  • Here, if $p>q$ (respectively $p<q$), we define $\beta_{q+1}=\dots =\beta_{p}=0$ (respectively, $\al_{p+1}=\dots =\al_{q}=0$)

1.1. GARCH(1,1)¶

  • To better understand properties of GARCH(p,q) models, let us focus on GARCH(1,1)
\begin{align*} \begin{cases} a_t = \sig_t\,\eps_t,\quad \eps_t\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} F_\eps,\\ \sig_t^2 = \om + \al_1\,a_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1\,\sig_{t-1}^2. \end{cases} \end{align*}
  • Let $\eta_t:=$ $a_t^2-$ $\sig_t^2$, then
\begin{align*} a_t^2 = \om + (\al_1+\beta_1) a_{t-1}^2 + \eta_t - \beta_1 \eta_{t-1}. \end{align*}
  • $\{a_t\}$ is weakly stationary if $\om\ge0,\al_1\ge0, \beta_1\le 1,$ and $\al_1+\beta_1<1$.
  • Volatility of $\{a_t\}$ clusters as in ARCH(1)
  • If $1-2\al_1^2$ $-(\al_1$ $+\beta_1)^2$ $>0$, then the kurtosis of $a_t$ is
\begin{align*} \frac{\Eb(a_t^4)}{\big(\Eb(a_t^2)\big)^2} = \frac{3 \big(1-(\al_1+\beta_1)^2\big)}{1-2\al_1^2-(\al_1+\beta_1)^2}>3 \end{align*}
  • That is, the distribution of $a_t$ has heavier tails than the normal distribution
  • Next, let us find forecasts of volatility $\sig_t$.
  • For finding the 1-step-ahead forecast, we write the volatility equation for $\sig_{t+1}^2$
\begin{align*} \sig_{t+1}^2 = \om + \al_1 a_t^2 + \beta_1 \sig_t^2. \end{align*}
  • So, the 1-step-ahead forecast for $\sig_{t+1}^2$ given $a_t, a_{t-1}, a_{t-2},...$ is
\begin{align*} \sigh_{t}^2(1) = \omh + \alh_1 a_t^2 + \betah_1 \sigh_t^2. \end{align*}
  • Here, $\alh_1$ and $\beta_1$ are estimates of $\al$ and $\beta$ (given $a_t, a_{t-1}, a_{t-2},...$).
  • Furthermore, $\sigh_t, \sigh_{t-1}, \dots, \sigh_{1}$ are calculated recursively using
\begin{align*} \sigh_t^2 = \omh + \alh_1\,a_{t-1}^2 + \betah_1\,\sigh_{t-1}^2 \end{align*}
  • To find 2-step-ahead forecast, we first replace $a_{t+1}^2=\sig_{t+1}^2\eps_{t+1}^2$ in the volatility equation
\begin{align*} \sig_{t+2}^2 &= \om + \al_1 a_{t+1}^2 + \beta_1 \sig_{t+1}^2\\\\ &= \om + \al_1 \sig_{t+1}^2 \eps_{t+1}^2 \color{red}{- \al_1 \sig_{t+1}^2 + \al_1 \sig_{t+1}^2} + \beta_1 \sig_{t+1}^2\\\\ &= \om + \al_1 \sig_{t+1}^2 (\eps_{t+1}^2-1) + (\al_1+\beta_1) \sig_{t+1}^2 \end{align*}
  • Noting that $\Eb(\eps_{t+1}^2$ $|a_{t},a_{t-1}$ $,\dots) = $ $\Eb($ $\eps_{t+1}^2)=$ $\Var(\eps_{t+1}$ $)=1$, we obtain
\begin{align*} \sigh_t^2(2) &= \omh + (\alh_1+\betah_1) \sigh_t^2(1) \end{align*}
  • Using a similar argument, we have for all $h\ge2$,
\begin{align*} \sigh_t^2(h) &= \omh + (\alh_1+\betah_1) \sigh_t^2(h-1) \end{align*}
  • Compare this result with the multi-step-ahead forecasts of an ARMA(1,1) model (Question 1.(a) of Homework 5)

2. Fitting ARIMA+GARCH models¶

  • An ARIMA+GARCH model is a time series model in which the mean equation is specified by an ARIMA model while the innovations (that is the error in the eqution for the time series) are specified by a GARCH model
  • Let us illustrate by using the DJI example from the previous lecture (note that now, we are looking at a longer time-series starting at Jan. 2007)
In [3]:
library("quantmod")
DJI = getSymbols("^DJI", src="yahoo", auto.assign=FALSE)$DJI.Adjusted
rtn = na.omit(diff(log(DJI)))
plot(rtn, type="l", col=1, main = "DJI returns")
  • The returns are stationary, but not weak WN
In [4]:
library(tseries)
par(mar=c(4.5,4.5,4.5,4.5))
acf(as.numeric(rtn), main="sample ACF of return")
kpss.test(rtn)
Box.test(rtn, lag = 5, type = "Ljung-Box")

tsdiag_vol = function(model, lag, fitdf, span=0.5){
    par(mfrow=c(1,2));par(mar=c(3,3,3,3))
    plot(resid(model)**2, type="l", col=1,
         main = expression(residual^2))
    smoother = loess((resid(model)**2) ~ seq(1,length(resid(model))),
                     span=span)
    lines(seq(1,length(resid(model))),fitted(smoother),col=2)
    acf((resid(model)**2), main=expression("sample ACF of "~ residual^2))
    Box.test(resid(model)**2, lag = lag, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = fitdf)
}
tsdiag_norm = function(model){
    qqnorm(resid(model), datax = FALSE,
       xlab = "normal quantile",
       ylab = "sample quantile of residuals",
       main = "normal probability plot for residuals")
    qqline(resid(model), datax=FALSE, col = 2)
    shapiro.test(resid(model))
}
  • Next, we test for the ARCH effect in the residuals of the MA(1) model. The volatility is not constant.
In [8]:
tsdiag_vol(fit, lag=12, fitdf=1, span=0.25)

	Box-Ljung test

data:  resid(model)^2
X-squared = 3676.3, df = 11, p-value < 2.2e-16
  • First, we consider an ARCH(p) model for the errors.
  • The PACF of the squared returns indicate ARCH order of 14 (at least).
  • We should consider GARCH to get a more parsimonous model
In [9]:
par(mar=c(4.5,4.5,4.5,4.5))
pacf(as.numeric(rtn**2), main=expression("sample PACF of "~ return^2))
  • Next, we fit an ARIMA(0,0,1)+GARCH(1,1) model
  • The fitted model is:
\begin{align*} \begin{cases} r_t = 7.164\,\times 10^{-04} + a_t - 0.058678\, a_{t-1};\quad a_t = \sig_t\eps_t,\quad \eps_t\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim}N(0,1)\\ \sig_t^2 = 2.411\times 10^{-6} + 0.13743\,a_{t-1}^2 + 0.8433\,\sig_{t-1}^2 \end{cases} \end{align*}
  • The test statistics show that the ARIMA+GARCH specification is adequet, thought the normality assumption does not hold
In [11]:
library(fGarch)
fit_magarch = garchFit(~arma(0,1)+garch(1,1), data=rtn, trace = F)
summary(fit_magarch)

3. Extensions of GARCH model¶

  • Next, we discuss some extensions of the GARCH model.
  • These models have been proposed to explain the characteristics of time series for which simple GARCH models are not appropriate

  • Specifically, we are interested in measuring the following characteristics of financial returns

    • Persistence shocks to vol: IGARCH

    • Risk premium: GARCH-M

    • Leverage effect: EGARCH, TGARCH, APARCH (Lecture 13)

3.1. Integrated GARCH (IGARCH)¶

  • An IGARCH(p,q) model is a GARCH(p,q) model in which the ARMA model for $\{a_t^2\}$ has a unit root
\begin{align*} a_t^2 = \om + \sum_{i=1}^{\max(p,q)} (\al_i+\beta_i) a_{t-i}^2 + \eta_t -\sum_{j=1}^q \beta_j \eta_{t-j} \end{align*}
  • In other words, the characteristic polynomial has complex root with $|x|\le 1$
\begin{align*} 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{\max(p,q)} (\al_i+\beta_i) x^i=0 \end{align*}
  • Recall that changes in the mean of ARIMA(p,1,q) processes are persistent
  • In a similar way, the impact of past volatility shocks in IGARCH(p,q) models is persistent. This is the key feature of IGARCH model.
  • Consider an IGARCH(1,1) model
\begin{align*} \begin{cases} a_t = \sig_t\,\eps_t,\quad \eps_t\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} F_\eps,\\ \sig_t^2 = \om + (1-\beta_1)\,a_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1\,\sig_{t-1}^2. \end{cases} \end{align*}
  • Here, we assume $0<\beta_1<1$.
  • Does the characteristic equation for the ARMA model of $\{a_t^2\}$ has a unit root?
  • Major difference between GARCH and IGARCH: the unconditional variance of an IGARCH process is not defined
  • Because IGARCH processes do not have second moment, they cannot be weakly stationary!
  • However, under additional conditions, they are strictly stationary
  • The same is true for the volatility process $\{\sig_t\}$ of an IGARCH process. It is not weakly stationary since it does not have the first two moments. However, under additional conditions, they are strictly stationary
  • Forecasting for IGARCH models is similar to GARCH
  • Consider the case of IGARCH(1,1)
  • Repeating the argument for multi-step-ahead forecasts of simple GARCH(1,1) yield, for $h\ge2$
\begin{align*} \sigh_t^2(h) &= \omh + (1-\betah_1+\betah_1) \sigh_t^2(h-1)\\\\ &= \omh + \sigh_t^2(h-1)\\\\ &= \omh + \omh + \sigh_t^2(h-2) = \dots = (h-1)\omh + \sigh_t^2(1) \end{align*}
  • The $h$-step-ahead vol forecast is a linear function of forecast horizon $h$ with slope $\omh$
  • If $\om=0$, then the multi-step-ahead vol forecast are constant (not changing with the forecast horizon $h$). This property is used in RiskMetrics which is the benchmark model for calculating Value-at-Risk
  • Let us consider monthly excess return of S&P 500. The data is in the text file "m-SP500.txt" which accompanies this lecture notes.
In [21]:
rtn = ts(read.table("m-SP500.txt", header=TRUE), start=c(1926,1), frequency=12)

  • auto.arima() suggests an MA(1) model for the mean equation.

In [23]:
tsdiag(fit)
  • The sample ACF plot of residuals$^2$ indicates ARCH effect
  • Both ACF and PACF of residuals$^2$ need high GARCH order. That is, the affect of shocks to vol seems persistent. To get a parsimonious model, we may try an IGARCH(1,1) model.
In [24]:
par(mfrow=c(1,2));par(mar=c(3,3,3,3))
acf(as.numeric(resid(fit)**2), lag.max=50)
pacf(as.numeric(resid(fit)**2), lag.max=50)
  • We use the rugarch package to fit MA+IGARCH model. This package is similar to fGarch, and is capable of fitting ARFIMA + several variations of GARCH model.
  • The fitted model is
\begin{align*} \begin{cases} r_t - 0.007431 = a_t + 0.035311 a_{t-1},\\ a_t = \sig_t\,\eps_t,\quad \eps_t\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} N(0,1),\\ \sig_t^2 = 0.000051 + 0.142869\,a_{t-1}^2 + 0.857131\,\sig_{t-1}^2. \end{cases} \end{align*}
  • Model diagnostic is as before. The mean and volatility equations seem adequate. The standardized residuals seem normally distributed.
In [26]:
library(rugarch)
spec = ugarchspec(variance.model=list(model="iGARCH", garchOrder=c(1,1)),
                  mean.model=list(armaOrder=c(0,1)))
fit_igarch = ugarchfit(data=rtn, spec=spec)
show(fit_igarch)

3.2. GARCH in the mean (GARCH-M)¶

  • It is generally accepted that the return of a financial assets depends on its volatility
  • Justification: Volatility is interpreted as a measure of risk in investing in an asset. Therefore, assets with higher volatility should have higher returns to compensate for their higher risk. The additional expected return (over, say, a risk-free asset) is called the risk premium
  • This justification is not completely accurate, actually. Only risk that cannot be diversified away (i.e. by investing in other assets) should be compensated. Pure gambling does not contribute to risk premium! (More on this when we study factor models.)
  • The GARCH-M model considers a mean equation of the form
\begin{align*} r_t = \mu + c\,g(\sig_t) + a_t \end{align*}
  • Here, the parameter $c$ is referred to as the risk premium and is expected to be positive.
  • Two common choices for the function $g(\cdot)$ is $g(\sig)=\sig$ and $g(\sig)=\sig^2$.
  • The volatility equation for $\sig_t^2$ can a GARCH, IGARCH, etc.
  • Let us fit a GARCH(1,1)-M model to monthly excess return of S&P 500 time series.
  • We can use archm=TRUE and archpow=2 (respectively, archpow=1) to add a GARCH-M term $c\,\sig_t^2)$ (respectively, $c\,\sig_t^2)$) to the mean equation.
\begin{align*} \begin{cases} r_t = 0.005421 + 1.007914\, \sig_t^2 + a_t,\\ a_t = \sig_t\,\eps_t,\quad \eps_t\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} N(0,1),\\ \sig_t^2 = 0.000083 + 0.123119\,a_{t-1}^2 + 0.852274\,\sig_{t-1}^2. \end{cases} \end{align*}
  • The estimated risk-premium is 1.007914. However, it is statistically insignificant.
In [30]:
spec = ugarchspec(variance.model=list(garchOrder=c(1,1)),
                  mean.model=list(armaOrder=c(0,0),
                                  archm=TRUE, archpow=2))
fit_garchm = ugarchfit(data=rtn, spec=spec)
show(fit_garchm)
